title: Beige Book — March 4, 2026
html:
Official report: Summary · Full PDF Local PDF: 2026-03-04 Beige Book.pdf

Overall economic activity

Activity rose at a slight to moderate pace in seven of twelve Districts, while five reported flat or declining activity. Manufacturing improved, with eight Districts reporting growth, helped by demand tied to data centers and energy infrastructure. Transportation was mixed. Residential real estate and construction softened, while nonresidential construction rose slightly. Financial services were stable to up, led by commercial lending. Energy grew modestly and agriculture was mostly flat. Businesses generally expected slight to moderate growth ahead.

Consumer spending

Consumer spending edged up, but uncertainty, price sensitivity, and weaker spending by lower-income households held sales back. Winter storms slowed retail traffic. Auto sales were mostly down, largely because of affordability concerns.

Labor markets

Employment was generally stable, with seven Districts reporting no change in hiring. Some firms cited higher nonlabor costs, softer demand, or uncertainty as reasons for flat or lower staffing. Firms are using AI and automation mainly to raise productivity rather than replace workers. Wages rose modestly or moderately, especially in the skilled trades, and health insurance premiums kept pushing up total compensation.

Prices

Prices rose moderately: eight Districts reported moderate increases and four reported slight or modest ones. Nonlabor costs rose for insurance, utilities, energy, metals, and other raw materials, and nine Districts cited tariffs. Many firms held selling prices steady despite higher costs because customers were more price-sensitive. Firms expected price growth to slow somewhat in the near term.

Notable themes

  • Data centers and energy infrastructure: a key driver of manufacturing demand.
  • Tariffs: cited by nine Districts as a cost factor.
  • Affordability: weighing on autos and lower-income households.
  • AI and automation: aimed at productivity, not job replacement.
  • Housing: residential softening; nonresidential construction up slightly.

District highlights

  • Boston: Flat activity; slight wage growth; moderate price increases; intense financial pressure on low-income families.
  • New York: Modest decline; flat employment; some consumers pausing major purchases.
  • Philadelphia: Modest growth; rising employment; low- to fixed-income households struggling.
  • Cleveland: Modest growth driven by manufacturing, commercial construction, and data centers.
  • Richmond: Modest growth; flat retail; stronger travel; declines in manufacturing and residential real estate.
  • Atlanta: Modest to moderate expansion; flat-to-down employment; improved housing demand.
  • Chicago: Slight growth; manufacturing up modestly; financial conditions loosening.
  • St. Louis: Unchanged but expected to rise; contacts cautiously optimistic.
  • Minneapolis: Slight decline in employment, consumer spending, manufacturing, and construction.
  • Kansas City: Slight growth; steady labor conditions; modest energy gains.
  • Dallas: Moderate expansion; strong manufacturing; weaker energy and agriculture; rising wages and prices.
  • San Francisco: Slight contraction; tech layoffs; weaker retail and services.

Read-through for SPY

  • Data center and energy-infrastructure demand lifting manufacturing supports the AI/industrial capex story that drives much of the index.
  • Firms absorbing higher costs rather than raising prices points to margin pressure for consumer-facing companies.
  • Expectations that price growth will ease slightly would be a modest positive for rate-sensitive stocks.
